name: Taplio
tagline: Plan LinkedIn content and maintain a manual relationship follow-up list

pricing.notes: Typical Starter monthly rate; product packaging can change.

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: 1 LinkedIn account; content scheduling and analytics; AI post writing is not included

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: 1 LinkedIn account; AI writing, engagement tools, relationship features and team collaboration
tiers.notes: Annual plan is billed $588/year; the public page does not state a numeric AI-generation allowance.

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.limits: 1 LinkedIn account; unlimited AI posts/comments, automated lead outreach and priority support

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; 7-day Pro trial and 30-day money-back guarantee
pricing.hiddenCosts: Pricing is per LinkedIn user/account. Starter omits the AI writer; Growth's AI allowance is not numerically disclosed; automated outreach requires Pro.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Taplio, plan LinkedIn content and maintain a manual relationship follow-up list. The hard boundary is linkedin data, inspiration feed, scheduling, relationship workflows, and analytics, plus api access, connector upkeep, and collaboration.
coreLoopDIY: Draft and schedule LinkedIn posts, preview them accurately, publish through one official API, maintain a manual relationship follow-up list, and retain a searchable content calendar.
requirements: developer application for one social network
whatYouLose: LinkedIn data, inspiration feed, scheduling, relationship workflows, and analytics
moatNotes: API access, connector upkeep, and collaboration
ongoingBurden: OAuth review, API policy changes, media limits, queues, retries, rate limits, webhooks, tokens, and moderation workflows
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Taplio because the scheduler is easy; staying approved and correct across constantly changing social APIs is the subscription. The recurring cost buys OAuth review, API policy changes, media limits, queues, retries, rate limits, webhooks, tokens, and moderation workflows, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Postiz
priorArt.desc: Active open-source social media scheduling platform.

rejectedAlternatives.name: BrightBean Studio
rejectedAlternatives.desc: It publishes LinkedIn and tracks results, but has no relationship follow-up list.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Buffer Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: LinkedIn scheduling and basic analytics, minus lead lists, relationship reminders and serious ideation.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Postiz
rejectedAlternatives.desc: AI-assisted LinkedIn publishing is covered; relationship management is not.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a single-network scheduler DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Taplio in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and one official social-platform API; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: draft and schedule LinkedIn posts, preview them accurately, publish through one official API, maintain a manual relationship follow-up list, and retain a searchable content calendar.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Support drafts, scheduled times, queues, campaigns, tags, and a weekly calendar.
Connect exactly one social network using its documented OAuth flow.
Validate character, media, aspect-ratio, and file-size limits before scheduling.
Publish through an idempotent background job with retries and clear failure states.
Store platform post identifiers and refresh publication status without scraping.
Add reusable snippets, local media storage, CSV export, and a token reconnect flow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out unofficial automation or scraping.
Deliberately leave out multi-network inbox and social listening.
Deliberately leave out agency approvals, white labelling, and enterprise reporting.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
